extracted.intended_audience: editors, contributors, and reviewers of literary and scientific periodicals; members and candidates of learned societies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the rights, responsibilities, and practical standards of journal editors and contributors (authorship, editorial alteration, reviewer competence), together with criteria for conduct and membership in learned societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility and control
rubrics_metrics.description: All that is in a journal, except what is marked as from a correspondent, is published entirely on editorial responsibility, as much as if the editor had written it himself; the editor may claim and exercise unlimited right of omission, addition, and alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor has final authority over content (including omitting or inserting material) and may perform last revises without the contributor's knowledge. This is the foundation for the editor's practical right to shape articles for the periodical's purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor as supplier of materials (no veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'contributor' implies that he furnishes materials without stating what he furnishes or how much of it is accepted; the editor does not acknowledge the contributor's right to withdraw an article if alterations are made in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors provide material expecting editorial discretion; requests for suppression would be refused if made as a demand. Contributors should therefore expect editorial modification and have limited rights to prevent publication once submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope of editorial intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor who meddles with substantive matter is likely to be wrong, even when he knows the subject; but one who prunes what he deems excess is likely to be right, even when he does not know the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should avoid substantive rewrites of technical argument but may and should prune excess for tone, length, or alignment with the journal's purpose. Excessive substantive meddling risks error; thoughtful pruning is generally defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of contributors for subject-matter competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors select contributors partly on the ground that the contributor is likely to 'know his business better than an editor can teach him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should prefer authors with demonstrable knowledge of the subject; this reduces the need for substantive editorial correction and preserves content quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor adaptation to periodical tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A contributor, knowing he is supplying an editor, learns, without suppressing truth or suggesting falsehood, to make the tone of his communications suit the periodical in which they are to appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for writers: tailor tone and presentation to the journal's established style while preserving truthfulness; this is a common and expected part of contributing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of last-minute insertions/omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight insertions or omissions made hurriedly by an editor on the last proof may contradict other parts of the article or render it unintelligible; the exact sting of an alteration may not be appreciated until after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should take care with last-minute edits; contributors should be aware that small changes can materially alter meaning, and both parties should be cautious about unattended proof-stage edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling allegations of authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked whether he wrote an article, a man may refuse to answer (regarded as admission), deny, or qualify—e.g., say the article was of his material but the editor has not let it stand as he gave it; he may decline to specify the extent of editorial interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on public responses: several strategies exist (refusal, denial, partial ownership) depending on conscience, reputation, and the amount of editorial alteration. Be mindful that absolute denials or admissions have moral and reputational implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to deny to protect secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: By analogy with property rights, when a man has a right to his secret, he has a right to all that is necessary to keep it; if he can only keep his secret by denial, he has a right to denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/legal justification for denying authorship or details in some cases (e.g., to protect a secret), though the text notes this answer only avails against others, not against the denier's own conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial handling of letters of complaint and correspondent material
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor is never of so editorial a mind as when revising the comments of a contributor upon an assailant of the article; there is often no time to send these letters to the contributor, and editors do not meddle with the letters of a correspondent except under notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will often edit or omit parts of complaint-letters and comments for responsibility and tone; contributors should not assume full control over published responses and should understand editorial prerogatives in contentious exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unauthorised insertions into signed letters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wrong for an editor to insert fiction or satirical matter into a signed letter without notice to the letter's author (an anecdote of an editor inserting satire in a signed letter is condemned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not forge or add content in correspondence that would misrepresent the signatory; doing so is an abuse of editorial power and may justify rebuke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reviewers/contributors to learn before teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: General expressions of slighting or contempt refer to the ignorant, 'who teach before they have learned.' Those of whom the author can speak with respect sought knowledge in the subject they were to handle before they completed their speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for good reviewing and public commentary: obtain requisite subject knowledge before publishing judgments or teaching; avoid premature or uninformed speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of exposing absurdities (satirical review as service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir John Hill's satire, by collecting the Royal Society's absurdities, was a benefactor of the Society because it showed that inquirers had actually been inquiring and exposed puerile research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One defensible editorial/reviewer stance is to expose and collect absurdities rather than softening them; such exposure can be beneficial for improving institutional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding principle for learned-society membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society was founded as a co-operative body; the qualification was ability and willingness to do good work for the promotion of natural knowledge, regardless of social position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical standard for evaluating candidates: merit and willingness to promote knowledge, not social rank or wealth. This is offered as a normative benchmark against later practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of competitive/elective limitation for society membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The election became a competitive examination limited to fifteen recommended by the Council; it shifted from 'Are you able and willing to promote natural knowledge?' to 'Are you one of the upper fifteen...?', potentially excluding worthy candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that competitive limits and oligarchic selection criteria may unjustly bar deserving investigators; societies should be cautious about turning fellowship into narrow competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to dues as a barrier to distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a condition precedent—four pounds a year or forty pounds down—to attach F.R.S. to a name; this creates a class-distinction where the honor can be worn only by those who can afford it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical critique: financial requirements for membership or status in learned societies create inequality and may distort the meaning of scientific distinction; membership practices should consider access and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic obligation to send 'best' work to an eminent society
rubrics_metrics.description: The author sees no more obligation for a contributor to send his best to the Royal Society than to himself; preference for a particular society is the contributor's choice, not a duty enforceable by the societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors retain autonomy to choose venue; eminent societies should not assume contributors owe them the best submissions as a matter of right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of philosophical error opposing observational error
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgar errors (pseudodoxes) are frequently opposed by scientific errors; good sense is always good sense, as shown in Browne's treatment of popular misconceptions (example: Amphisbæna).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical work should distinguish between popular misconception and scientific fallacy; both sorts of error require different responses but common-sense reasoning is valuable across cases.
